title: Femoral neck fracture and avascular necrosis
text:
Intracapsular neck fractures in osteoporotic elderly patients tear the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery, which run up the neck beneath the synovium. The femoral head can undergo avascular necrosis, so displaced intracapsular fractures are usually treated by arthroplasty rather than fixation. The leg lies shortened and externally rotated.
Extracapsular (intertrochanteric) fractures spare the head's blood supply and heal well with fixation.

title: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis and Perthes disease
text:
SCFE: the epiphysis slips posteriorly and inferiorly through the growth plate in overweight adolescents (or with hypothyroidism); pain is often referred to the knee, and hip flexion forces the thigh into external rotation.
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease: idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children aged 4 to 8, causing a painless limp and later flattening of the head.

title: Tibial fractures and compartment syndrome
text:
The anteromedial tibia is subcutaneous, so shaft fractures are frequently open, and its distal third has a poor blood supply prone to delayed union.
The leg's tight osteofascial compartments make tibial fractures the commonest cause of acute compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch of the muscles and tense compartments. Pulses usually persist until very late. Untreated, it causes muscle necrosis and Volkmann contracture; treatment is urgent fasciotomy.
Osgood-Schlatter disease is traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity in adolescent athletes.

title: Fibular neck injury and ankle fractures
text:
The common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck, so fractures there, tight casts or prolonged leg crossing produce foot drop.
Weber classification of lateral malleolar fractures: A below the syndesmosis (stable), B at the level of the syndesmosis, C above it (syndesmosis disrupted, unstable). A Maisonneuve fracture is a proximal fibular fracture with medial ankle injury and syndesmotic tear.

title: Patellar dislocation and patellofemoral pain
text:
The patella almost always dislocates laterally, because the quadriceps pulls along the femoral shaft axis (the Q-angle) and the lateral femoral condyle can be shallow. Vastus medialis obliquus and the medial patellofemoral ligament resist this; the MPFL tears in most first-time dislocations.
A bipartite patella (unfused superolateral ossification centre) can be mistaken for a fracture.

title: Talar neck fracture
text: Most of the talus is covered by articular cartilage, and its blood supply enters mainly through the neck and sinus tarsi (artery of the tarsal canal). Neck fractures from forced dorsiflexion ('aviator's astragalus') carry a high risk of avascular necrosis of the body, which rises with each Hawkins grade of displacement. Preserved subchondral lucency at 6 to 8 weeks (Hawkins sign) indicates revascularisation.

title: Calcaneal fractures
text:
Axial loading from a fall from height crushes the calcaneus, flattening Böhler's angle and disrupting the subtalar joint. About 10% are associated with vertebral (thoracolumbar) burst fractures, so the spine must be checked. Long-term subtalar arthritis is common.
Posterior heel pain in adolescents may be calcaneal apophysitis (Sever disease).

title: Navicular stress fracture and accessory navicular
text:
The central third of the navicular is relatively avascular, so stress fractures in sprinters and jumpers heal poorly and are easily missed on plain films.
An accessory navicular within the tibialis posterior tendon can cause medial foot pain and is associated with flatfoot. Köhler disease is avascular necrosis of the navicular in young children.

title: Foot drop
text:
The most commonly injured nerve of the lower limb, vulnerable as it winds around the fibular neck (fracture, plaster cast, crossed legs, prolonged squatting, rapid weight loss). Deep fibular loss paralyses dorsiflexors, so the foot slaps and the patient lifts the knee high (steppage gait); superficial fibular loss removes eversion. Sensation is lost on the dorsum of the foot and first web space.
Eversion is preserved and inversion weak in an L5 radiculopathy, which helps distinguish it from a fibular nerve lesion.

title: Sciatic nerve injury
text:
Posterior hip dislocation, acetabular fractures and misplaced gluteal injections (in the upper outer quadrant is safe) can damage the nerve. Loss of hamstrings and all muscles below the knee leaves a flail foot and sensory loss below the knee except the medial leg (saphenous). The fibular division is more superficial and more often affected than the tibial division.
Piriformis syndrome describes compression where the nerve passes below or through piriformis.

title: Femoral nerve injury
text: Injured by pelvic and hip surgery, retroperitoneal (iliopsoas) haematoma in anticoagulated patients, or lithotomy positioning. Quadriceps paralysis makes the knee buckle, the patellar reflex is lost and sensation fails over the anterior thigh and, via the saphenous nerve, the medial leg and foot.

title: Tarsal tunnel syndrome
text: Compression of the tibial nerve beneath the flexor retinaculum behind the medial malleolus (by ganglia, varicosities, tenosynovitis or valgus hindfoot) causes burning pain and paraesthesia in the sole, worse at night and with standing. The medial calcaneal branch often arises proximal to the tunnel, sparing the heel.

title: Meralgia paraesthetica
text: Compression of the nerve as it passes under or through the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine (tight belts, obesity, pregnancy, prolonged sitting or hip positioning) produces burning numbness of the anterolateral thigh with no motor weakness.

title: Obturator nerve injury
text: Can be injured by pelvic fractures, obturator hernia, pelvic lymph node dissection or compressed by the fetal head in labour. Adductor weakness produces a wide-based circumducting gait and a small area of numbness on the medial thigh. Hip pain may be referred to the medial knee along the same nerve, a classic pitfall in children with hip disease.

title: ACL rupture
text:
Non-contact pivoting or landing injuries with valgus and rotation; the patient often feels a pop and develops a haemarthrosis within hours. Anterior tibial translation is detected by the Lachman test (most sensitive) and anterior drawer; the pivot-shift test demonstrates rotational instability.
The O'Donoghue 'unhappy triad' pairs ACL rupture with medial collateral ligament and meniscal injury. Chronic instability accelerates meniscal tears and osteoarthritis. A Segond fracture (lateral tibial avulsion) is almost pathognomonic.

title: PCL injury (dashboard injury)
text: A posteriorly directed blow to the proximal tibia with the knee flexed, typically striking a car dashboard, tears the PCL. Posterior sag of the tibia and a positive posterior drawer are seen. Check for associated posterior hip dislocation and posterolateral corner injury.

title: Meniscal tears
text:
Twisting on a weight-bearing flexed knee tears the menisci. The medial meniscus is torn more often because it is attached to the medial collateral ligament and capsule and is less mobile. A displaced bucket-handle tear causes true locking (inability to fully extend).
Only the peripheral third (red zone) is vascularised, so peripheral tears can be repaired whereas inner tears are trimmed. Degenerative tears are common in older knees and often asymptomatic.

title: MCL sprain
text: Valgus force to the knee (a tackle from the lateral side) tears the tibial collateral ligament, the most commonly injured knee ligament. Isolated tears usually heal non-operatively owing to the ligament's good blood supply. Its deep fibres blend with the medial meniscus, linking the two injuries. Pellegrini-Stieda lesion: calcification at the femoral origin after injury.

title: Lateral ankle sprain
text: Inversion with plantarflexion tears the anterior talofibular ligament first (the weakest lateral ligament), then the calcaneofibular ligament. Repeated sprains cause chronic lateral instability and peroneal tendon injury. The Ottawa ankle rules identify patients who need radiographs to exclude fracture (e.g. of the base of the fifth metatarsal).

title: Achilles tendon rupture
text: Typically ruptures 2 to 6 cm above its insertion, a hypovascular watershed, in middle-aged recreational athletes, or after fluoroquinolone or corticosteroid use. Patients describe being kicked in the heel. The Thompson (Simmonds) test is positive: squeezing the calf fails to plantarflex the foot. Weak plantarflexion may persist through the long toe flexors, which can mislead examiners.

title: Trendelenburg sign
text: Gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve) hold the pelvis level when standing on one leg. Weakness, nerve injury (e.g. from a misplaced injection or hip surgery), hip dislocation or a coxa vara make the pelvis drop on the opposite, unsupported side. The patient compensates by lurching the trunk over the stance leg (Trendelenburg gait). Tendinopathy of the gluteus medius insertion causes greater trochanteric pain syndrome.

title: Plantar fasciitis
text: Degenerative enthesopathy of the plantar aponeurosis at its origin on the medial calcaneal tubercle; first-step pain in the morning is characteristic. Associated with obesity, prolonged standing, running and tight calf muscles. Heel spurs are often coexistent but are not the cause of pain. Plantar fibromatosis (Ledderhose disease) is the counterpart of Dupuytren contracture.

title: Varicose veins and graft use
text:
Incompetence of the saphenofemoral junction valve lets blood reflux down the great saphenous vein, dilating its tributaries along the medial leg. Chronic venous hypertension leads to oedema, haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis and venous ulcers above the medial malleolus.
Because of its length and superficial position the vein is the standard conduit for coronary artery bypass grafts, and it is used for venous cutdown anterior to the medial malleolus. The saphenous nerve runs alongside and can be injured during stripping.

title: Popliteal artery aneurysm and knee dislocation
text:
The popliteal artery is tethered at the adductor hiatus and soleal arch, so knee dislocations frequently intimal-tear or transect it: an ankle-brachial index must be checked in all dislocations.
Popliteal aneurysms are the commonest peripheral aneurysm, often bilateral and associated with abdominal aortic aneurysm; they thrombose or embolise rather than rupture, threatening the limb.
Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome (aberrant medial head of gastrocnemius) causes claudication in young athletes.

title: Femoral artery access and peripheral arterial disease
text:
The common femoral artery at the mid-inguinal point, over the femoral head, is the standard site for arterial catheterisation; punctures above the inguinal ligament risk retroperitoneal haemorrhage and those below risk pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula.
The superficial femoral artery in the adductor canal is the commonest site of atherosclerotic occlusion causing calf claudication.
